query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

cited_evidence.text: The development of Pt-based catalysts for use in fuel cells that meet performance targets of high activity, maximized stability, and low cost remains a huge challenge. Herein, we report a nitrogen (N)-doped high-entropy alloy (HEA) electrocatalyst that consists of a Pt-rich shell and a N-doped PtCoFeNiCu core on a carbon support (denoted as N–Pt/HEA/C). The N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst showed a high mass activity of 1.34 A mgPt–1 at 0.9 V for the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) in rotating disk electrode (RDE) testing, which substantially outperformed commercial Pt/C and most of the other binary/ternary Pt-based catalysts. The N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst also demonstrated excellent stability in both RDE and membrane electrode assembly (MEA) testing. Using operando X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) measurements and theoretical calculations, we revealed that the enhanced ORR activity of N–Pt/HEA/C originated from the optimized adsorption energy of intermediates, resulting in the tailored electronic structure formed upon N-doping. Furthermore, we showed that the multiple metal–nitrogen bonds formed synergistically improved the corrosion resistance of the 3d transition metals and enhanced the ORR dur

Significantly, compared to binary or ternary alloys (e.g., solid-solution and intermetallic Pt alloys), HEA provides a broad binding energy distribution due to the large flexibility composition enabling a wide range of adsorption sites for multistep reaction (e.g., ORR), thereby achieving extraordinary catalytic performance.− The high entropy alloy also lowers the Gibbs free energy, which results in a more positive redox potential and consequently leads to enhanced stability of HEA catalysts. Additionally, nitrogen (N)-doping effects fine-tune the adsorption energetics of intermediates and improve the corrosion resistance by exploiting the pinning effect from the N atom to the coordinated metal atoms. The formation of metal–nitrogen bonds (M–N) has been well documented and their beneficial effect on catalytic activity and stability demonstrated in our previous studies (Ni–N, Co–N, Cu–N, and Fe–N). Based on the above discussion, the origin of the improved ORR performance of the N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst can be explained as follows. First, compared with pure Pt, the high-entropy structure with a Pt-rich surface not only adjusts the adsorption energies of *O and *OH on the Pt/HEA and N–Pt/HEA surfaces, which support an enhanced electron transfer efficiency for the ORR, but also reduces OH poisoning, resulting directly in the high ORR activity of the HEA catalysts. Second, the N-doping could further regulate the binding strength during the intermediate transformation and consequently contribute to boosting the ORR activity and stability of the N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst. Third, the chemically stable multiple M–N bonds, particularly Ni–N and Co–N, could greatly suppress the dissolution/oxidization of the TMs, while the optimized electronic structure of surface Pt due to the introduced N atoms could inhibit the dissolution of the Pt shell, which synergistically enhances the durability of the N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst.
